{{Short description|Time at which a random variable stops exhibiting a behavior of interest}}
{{for|the musical phenomenon|stop-time}}
{{Dark mode invert|[[Image:HittingTimes1.png|thumb|300px|Example of a stopping time: a [[hitting time]] of [[Brownian motion]]. The process starts at 0 and is stopped as soon as it hits 1.]]}}

In [[probability theory]], in particular in the study of [[stochastic process]]es, a '''stopping time''' (also '''Markov time''', '''Markov moment''', '''optional stopping time''' or '''optional time'''<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kallenberg |first1=Olav |author-link1=Olav Kallenberg |year=2017  |title=Random Measures, Theory and Applications|volume=77 |location= Switzerland |publisher=Springer |doi= 10.1007/978-3-319-41598-7|isbn=978-3-319-41596-3|pages=347|series=Probability Theory and Stochastic Modelling }} </ref>) is a specific type of "random time": a [[random variable]] whose value is interpreted as the time at which a given stochastic process exhibits a certain behavior of interest. A stopping time is often defined by a '''stopping rule''', a mechanism for deciding whether to continue or stop a process on the basis of the present position and past events, and which will [[almost always]] lead to a decision to stop at some finite time.

Stopping times occur in [[decision theory]], and the [[optional stopping theorem]] is an important result in this context. Stopping times are also frequently applied in mathematical proofs to "tame the continuum of time", as Chung put it in his book (1982).

==Definition==
=== Discrete time ===
Let <math> \tau </math> be a random variable, which is defined on the [[filtered probability space]] <math> (\Omega, \mathcal F, (\mathcal F_n)_{n \in \N}, P) </math> with values in <math> \mathbb N \cup \{ +\infty \}</math>. Then <math> \tau </math> is called a stopping time (with respect to the [[Filtration (probability theory)|filtration]] <math> \mathbb F= ((\mathcal F_n)_{n \in \N} )</math>) if the following condition holds:
:<math> \{ \tau =n \} \in \mathcal F_n </math> for all <math> n </math>
Intuitively, this condition means that the "decision" of whether to stop at time <math>n</math> must be based only on the information present at time <math>n</math>, not on any future information.

=== General case ===
Let <math> \tau </math> be a random variable, which is defined on the [[filtered probability space]] <math> (\Omega, \mathcal F, (\mathcal F_t)_{t \in T}, P) </math> with values in <math> T</math>. In most cases, <math> T=[0,+ \infty) </math>. Then <math> \tau </math> is called a stopping time (with respect to the [[Filtration (probability theory)|filtration]] <math> \mathbb F= (\mathcal F_t)_{t \in T} </math>), if the following condition holds:
:<math> \{ \tau \leq t \} \in \mathcal F_t </math> for all <math> t \in T </math>

=== As adapted process ===
Let <math> \tau </math> be a random variable, which is defined on the [[filtered probability space]] <math> (\Omega, \mathcal F, (\mathcal F_t)_{t \in T}, P) </math> with values in <math> T</math>. Then <math> \tau </math> is called a stopping time if the [[stochastic process]] <math> X=(X_t)_{t \in T}</math>, defined by
:<math> X_t:= \begin{cases} 1 & \text{ if } t < \tau \\ 0 &\text{ if } t \geq \tau \end{cases} </math>

is [[adapted process|adapted]] to the filtration <math> \mathbb F= (\mathcal F_t)_{t \in T}</math>

=== Comments ===
Some authors explicitly exclude cases where <math> \tau </math> can be <math> + \infty </math>, whereas other authors allow <math> \tau </math> to take any value in the closure of <math> T</math>.

==Examples==
To illustrate some examples of random times that are stopping rules and some that are not, consider a gambler playing [[roulette]] with a typical house edge, starting with $100 and betting $1 on red in each game:

*Playing exactly five games corresponds to the stopping time ''τ''&nbsp;=&nbsp;5, and ''is'' a stopping rule.
*Playing until they either run out of money or have played 500 games ''is'' a stopping rule.
*Playing until they obtain the maximum amount ahead they will ever be ''is not'' a stopping rule and does not provide a stopping time, as it requires information about the future as well as the present and past.
*Playing until they either double their money or run out of money ''is'' a stopping rule, even though there is potentially no limit to the number of games they play, but the probability that they stop in a finite time is 1.

To illustrate the more general definition of stopping time, consider [[Brownian motion]], which is a stochastic process <math>(B_t)_{t\geq 0}</math>, where each <math>B_t</math> is a random variable defined on the probability space <math>(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})</math>. We define a filtration on this probability space by letting <math>\mathcal{F}_t</math> be the ''&sigma;''-algebra generated by all the sets of the form <math>(B_s)^{-1}(A)</math> where <math>0\leq s \leq t</math> and <math>A\subseteq \mathbb{R}</math> is a [[Borel set]]. Intuitively, an event ''E'' is in <math>\mathcal{F}_t</math> if and only if we can determine whether ''E'' is true or false just by observing the Brownian motion from time 0 to time ''t''. 
* Every constant <math>\tau:=t_0</math> is (trivially) a stopping time; it corresponds to the stopping rule "stop at time <math>t_0</math>".
* Let <math>a\in\mathbb{R}.</math> Then <math>\tau:=\inf \{t\geq 0 \mid B_t = a\}</math> is a stopping time for Brownian motion, corresponding to the stopping rule: "stop as soon as the Brownian motion hits the value ''a''."
* Another stopping time is given by <math>\tau:=\inf \{t\geq 1 \mid B_s > 0 \text{ for all } s\in[t-1,t]\}</math>. It corresponds to the stopping rule "stop as soon as the Brownian motion has been positive over a contiguous stretch of length 1 time unit."
* In general, if τ<sub>1</sub> and τ<sub>2</sub> are stopping times on <math>\left(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \left\{ \mathcal{F}_{t} \right \}_{t \geq 0}, \mathbb{P}\right)</math> then their minimum <math>\tau _1 \wedge \tau _2</math>, their maximum <math>\tau _1 \vee \tau _2</math>, and their sum ''τ''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''τ''<sub>2</sub> are also stopping times. (This is not true for differences and products, because these may require "looking into the future" to determine when to stop.)

[[Hitting time]]s like the second example above can be important examples of stopping times. While it is relatively straightforward to show that essentially all stopping times are hitting times,<ref name="Fischer (2013)">{{cite journal|last=Fischer|first=Tom|title=On simple representations of stopping times and stopping time sigma-algebras|journal=Statistics and Probability Letters|year=2013|volume=83|issue=1|pages=345–349|doi=10.1016/j.spl.2012.09.024|arxiv=1112.1603}}</ref> it can be much more difficult to show that a certain hitting time is a stopping time. The latter types of results are known as the [[Hitting time#Début theorem|Début theorem]].

==Localization==
Stopping times are frequently used to generalize certain properties of stochastic processes to situations in which the required property is satisfied in only a local sense. First, if ''X'' is a process and τ is a stopping time, then ''X''<sup>''τ''</sup> is used to denote the process ''X'' stopped at time ''τ''.
:<math> X^\tau_t=X_{\min(t,\tau)}</math>
Then, ''X'' is said to locally satisfy some property ''P'' if there exists a sequence of stopping times τ<sub>''n''</sub>, which increases to infinity and for which the processes 
:<math>\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_n>0\}}X^{\tau_n}</math> 
satisfy property ''P''. Common examples, with time index set ''I'' = [0, ∞), are as follows:

<blockquote>'''Local martingale process'''. A process ''X'' is a [[local martingale]] if it is [[càdlàg]]{{what|reason= This appears to contradict the definition given in the article Local Martingale, where cadlag is not required.|date=October 2023}}  and there exists a sequence of stopping times τ<sub>''n''</sub> increasing to infinity, such that 
:<math>\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_n>0\}}X^{\tau_n}</math> 
is a [[martingale (probability theory)|martingale]] for each ''n''.</blockquote>

<blockquote>'''Locally integrable process'''. A non-negative and increasing process ''X'' is locally integrable if there exists a sequence of stopping times ''τ''<sub>''n''</sub> increasing to infinity, such that 
:<math>\operatorname{E} \left [\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_n>0\}}X^{\tau_n} \right ]<\infty</math> 
for each ''n''.</blockquote>

==Types of stopping times==
Stopping times, with time index set ''I'' = [0,∞), are often divided into one of several types depending on whether it is possible to predict when they are about to occur.

A stopping time ''τ'' is '''predictable''' if it is equal to the limit of an increasing sequence of stopping times ''τ''<sub>''n''</sub> satisfying ''τ''<sub>''n''</sub> < ''τ'' whenever ''τ'' > 0. The sequence ''τ''<sub>''n''</sub> is said to ''announce'' ''τ'', and predictable stopping times are sometimes known as ''announceable''.
Examples of predictable stopping times are [[hitting time]]s of continuous and [[Adapted process|adapted]] processes. If ''τ'' is the first time at which a continuous and real valued process ''X'' is equal to some value ''a'', then it is announced by the sequence ''τ''<sub>''n''</sub>, where ''τ''<sub>''n''</sub> is the first time at which ''X'' is within a distance of 1/''n'' of ''a''.

'''Accessible''' stopping times are those that can be covered by a sequence of predictable times. That is, stopping time ''τ'' is accessible if, P(''τ'' = ''τ''<sub>''n''</sub> for some ''n'') = 1, where ''τ''<sub>''n''</sub> are predictable times.

A stopping time ''τ'' is '''totally inaccessible''' if it can never be announced by an increasing sequence of stopping times. Equivalently, P(''τ'' = ''σ'' < ∞) = 0 for every predictable time ''σ''. Examples of totally inaccessible stopping times include the jump times of [[Poisson process]]es.

Every stopping time ''τ'' can be uniquely decomposed into an accessible and totally inaccessible time. That is, there exists a unique accessible stopping time σ and totally inaccessible time υ such that ''τ'' = ''σ'' whenever ''σ'' < ∞, ''τ'' = ''υ'' whenever ''υ'' < ∞, and ''τ'' = ∞ whenever ''σ'' = ''υ'' = ∞. Note that in the statement of this decomposition result, stopping times do not have to be almost surely finite, and can equal&nbsp;∞.

==Stopping rules in clinical trials==
Clinical trials in medicine often perform interim analysis, in order to determine whether the trial has already met its endpoints.
However, interim analysis create the risk of false-positive results, and therefore stopping boundaries are used to determine the number and timing of interim analysis (also known as alpha-spending, to denote the rate of false positives).
At each of R interim tests, the trial is stopped if the likelihood is below a threshold p, which depends on the method used. See [[Sequential analysis]].
